background.definition: Hemophilia is a bleeding disorder due to a deficiency of coagulation factors VIII or IX or due to antibodies inhibiting their function. Hemophilia A is the result of factor VIII deficiency and hemophilia B is due to factor IX deficiency.

list.listitem: The CDC reports an incidence rate of approximately 1 in 4300 live male births.

Compared to the US population, hemophilia is over-represented in patients who identify as White, equivalent in patients of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, and occurs less frequently in patients who identify as Black/African American.
The incidence of acquired hemophilia A is 1.5 cases per million persons per year.
Hemophilia A: 17.1 per 100,000 males.
Hemophilia B: 3.8 per 100,000 males.
A 2020 study estimated that 30,000 people in the U.S. have hemophilia.
More than 90% of the costs of hemophilia are due to the costs for drug treatment. Since the disease is rare, the global societal cost ranks quite low while the cost per patient is high.
Hemophilia is the most common severe bleeding disorder.

People with hemophilia have a higher prevalence of depression (odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.64-3.68), anxiety (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.01-3.00), anxiety/depression (OR 2.60, 95% CI 2.35-2.87) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (OR 3.48, 95% CI 1.74-6.96) then the general population.
Hemophilia A is a deficiency of coagulation factor VIII.
Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is a deficiency of coagulation factor IX.

Hemophilia is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder. Approximately one third of congenital hemophilia cases are due to new mutations, while in two thirds of cases there is a family history of the disease.
Rarely, hemophilia A can occur as an acquired autoimmune disorder due to autoantibody production against autologous factor VIII.
Factors VIII and IX are essential components of the coagulation cascade, mainly in the amplification phase.
Patients with hemophilia show a reduced ability to produce the thrombin burst necessary to produce a stable clot.

Risk_Factor.Risk_OR: Male child 50% will have hemophilia. Female child 50% will be carrier
Male child 0% will have hemophilia. Female child 100% will be carrier

list.listitem: Women with a family history of hemophilia should be offered genetic counseling. C
All patients with hemophilia treated with clotting factor concentrate prior to 1985 should be screened for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV infections. C
The factor VIII/IX level should be measured in all men with a family history of hemophilia and in all persons with a nontraumatic hemarthrosis.

The daughters of patients with hemophilia are carriers of hemophilia and should have their factor VIII/IX measured to establish their baseline coagulation factor concentration. Some carriers have factor VIII/IX levels below the lower limit of normal.

Hemophilia A and B can be confirmed by the identification of reduced concentrations of factors VIII and IX, respectively. The activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged in both, but the prothrombin time, fibrinogen, and platelet count are normal. C
Approximately 80% of patients with hemophilia present with hemarthroses. C
Hemophilia A and B are indistinguishable clinically. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Lifelong history of bleeding in joints or muscles (spontaneous and traumatic); delayed surgical bleeding
Marked skin bruising and muscular bleeds in previously healthy individuals
Usually secondary to other autoimmune diseases, malignancy or pregnancy
Bruising and mucosal bleeding; affects both sexes; no hemarthroses
Bruising and petechiae; family history with both sexes affected
Factor VIII/IX normal with other clotting deficiencies found
History of alcohol or drug use or viral hepatitis; bruising more prominent than joint bleeds
Acquired condition; abnormal liver enzymes; abnormal PT/INR values or platelet function tests

list.listitem:
Classification of the severity of hemophilia A and B is based on the level of the involved factors:
Severe: Less than 1% of normal factor VIII or IX level Moderate: 1% to 5% of normal factor VIII or IX level Mild: between 5% and 40% of normal factor VIII or IX level

Patients typically present with bruising (common in young children), hemarthroses, bleeding into muscles, hematuria, bleeding after dental extractions, and bleeding after surgery. Patients with severe disease present in early childhood, but those with mild disease can present at any age.
Ask for any family history of a sex-linked disorder of excessive bleeding, but it may not exist.

Approximately 80% of patients with hemophilia present with hemarthroses, 9% with soft tissue bleeding, 4% with bleeding of lips and gums, and approximately 1% with epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleeding, or hematuria.
Approximately one-third of hemarthroses occur in the knee, 20% in the ankle, 12% in the elbow, and 5% in the shoulder and hip.
During an acute hemarthrosis, the joint is typically hot, swollen, and painful to move. However, there may be no signs at all, even during an acute hemarthrosis.
In a small study of 7 patients with severe hemophilia, physical examination of the knees, ankles, and elbows only correlated with MRI findings approximately one-third of the time.
Among patients with joint symptoms (pain, tenderness, swelling, or locking), the presence of joint symptoms was 84% sensitive and 76% specific compared with MRI.
Cerebral bleeding after even minor injury must be considered because it is common and potentially fatal.
See for a summary of the diagnostic approach to the patient with suspected hemophilia.
If hemophilia is suspected, request a complete blood count and clotting screen (PT, APTT, fibrinogen).

If the APTT is prolonged, request mixing studies to differentiate between inherited and antibody-mediated acquired factor deficiency. Also request assays of factor VIII, factor IX, and von Willebrand factor.
An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for factor VIII antibodies, compared with the gold standard Bethesda assay, is 100% sensitive and 97.8% specific in patients with hemophilia A.

Thrombin generation and whole blood viscoelastic assays, known as global assays, provide more detailed information about thrombin generation and clot formation and can be used to investigate hemophilic phenotype and potential response to treatment.

No radiologic investigations are required for acute hemarthroses. Ultrasound scanning can confirm the diagnosis and quantify bleeding. Ultrasound is highly reliable for assessing soft-tissue abnormalities of ankles and knees, and substantially to highly reliable for assessing osteochondral changes in joints compared to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Patients with recurring or chronic joint complaints may warrant imaging.
MRI can be used to identify synovial hypertrophy and abnormal articular cartilage (seen in both symptomatic and asymptomatic joints).

Muscle hematomas that fail to settle quickly should undergo imaging with ultrasound scanning or CT. Head CT should be requested for patients with severe hemophilia after a head injury to exclude cerebral hematoma.

A challenge test with DDAVP (0.3 mcg/kg) should be performed in patients with mild hemophilia to identify those who are likely to respond to DDAVP therapy. In 62 boys with mild hemophilia A, 29 (47%) had a rise in factor VIII activity 1 hour after DDAVP administration.
In one study, circulating soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (sVCAM-1) identified in peripheral blood of patients with hemophilia A were associated with the severity of hemophilic arthropathy.
See for a suggested approach to evaluating patients with suspected hemophilia.
Management of most comorbid conditions is usually unchanged, other than avoidance of intramuscular injections and correction of the coagulopathy prior to invasive procedures or surgery.
Children with severe hemophilia should receive regular prophylactic factor VIII or IX concentrate to prevent bleeding and reduce morbidity.A
Patients with severe hemophilia should be treated with clotting factor concentrate on the first suspicion of a joint or muscle bleed. B
Patients with acquired hemophilia should receive immediate treatment with a factor VIII inhibitor bypassing agent (FEIBA) when actively bleeding and immunosuppression to eliminate the antibody.B
Patients with mild congenital hemophilia A who respond to a DDAVP challenge can be treated with DDAVP. C
Emicizumab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody that significantly reduces bleeding episodes in patients with inhibitors (alloantibodies) to factor VIII. B
Emicizumab is also available for use in patients without inhibitors where it has the advantage of subcutaneous administration. C
Gene therapy has been successfully used to treat hemophilia A and B in small Phase 1/2 dose ranging studies and more recently, in phase 3 studies as well.B

Patients with severe hemophilia A or B should be taught to self-infuse clotting factor concentrate as soon as a bleed is suspected. Parents should be educated to infuse the clotting factor to their children 3 times a week—25 to 50 IU per kg factor VIII or 40 IU per kg factor IX—as bleeding prophylaxis.

A 2025 Cochrane review found that prophylactically treating children with hemophilia A or B who had no known joint bleeding with Factor VIII or Factor IX concetrate may reduce the risk of hemarthrosis.

listitem.strong: Factor VIII concentrate for hemophilia A

list.listitem: Patients with severe and moderate congenital hemophilia A should receive factor VIII concentrate (plasma derived or recombinant).

In an RCT of children aged 1 to 7 years, those randomized to prophylactic therapy had fewer hemarthroses than children on episodic therapy (0.20 vs. 0.52 events per patient per month) and fewer radiologic signs of arthropathy (29% vs. 74%, respectively).Another RCT demonstrated that patients randomized to either 12 months of standard or pharmacokinetic-tailored every third day prophylaxis had comparable safety and effectiveness and reduced bleeding compared with on-demand treatment. These findings are supported by a prospective cohort study of 286 males with hemophilia in which the 17% of patients who received secondary prophylaxis had significantly fewer hemarthroses. There were no differences, however, in improvement in target joint range of motion or new target joint development. A Cochrane review found 6 randomized trials with 142 patients that showed significant reductions in bleeding events and joint bleeds.

Different preparations are available, including long-acting drugs allowing twice-weekly administration, but it is not clear that these will result in reduced development of neutralizing antibodies, and they are more costly. In a recent trial, about 15% to 30% of patients develop neutralizing anti-factor VIII alloantibodies (inhibitors) following replacement therapy. In one study, patients treated with plasma-derived factor VIII containing von Willebrand factor had a lower incidence of inhibitors than those treated with recombinant factor VIII.
Patients with mild congenital hemophilia A who respond to a DDAVP challenge can be treated with DDAVP. Nonresponders should receive factor VIII concentrate.

listitem.strong: Factor IX concentrate for hemophilia B

list.listitem: Patients with congenital hemophilia B of all severities should receive factor IX concentrate (plasma derived or recombinant).
A Cochrane review found 6 randomized trials with 142 patients that showed significant reductions in bleeding events and joint bleeds.
Patients who develop inhibitory antibodies to factor VIII or factor IX should receive Factor Eight Inhibitor Bypassing Acitivity (FEIBA) or recombinant factor VIIa concentrate to treat bleeding.

Two small trials were identified in a Cochrane review evaluating the relative effectiveness of recombinant factor VIIa concentrate compared with human plasma-derived concentrates in people with hemophilia and inhibiting antibodies—no differences were found in hemostatic effect.

Emicizumab is a monoclonal antibody that significantly reduces bleeding episodes in patients with inhibitors (alloantibodies) to Factor VIII. In a randomized trial, the rate of bleeding was significantly lower (3 vs. 23 bleeding events per year, p < 0.001). Adverse events were primarily injection site related, with two patients developing thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis.

Concizumab is an anti-tissue factor pathway inhibitor for patients with hemophilia A or B and inhibitors. In an RCT with 133 patients, patients given concizumab had significantly fewer bleeding events (1.7 vs 11.8/year, p < .001).

Based largely on data from uncontrolled studies, patients with acquired hemophilia A should receive FEIBA, porcine FVIII or recombinant factor VIIa concentrate to treat acute bleeding. Additionally, they should receive steroids plus oral cyclophosphamide or rituximab to eradicate the autoantibody.
Tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid are useful for mucosal bleeding (except urogenital).

There is insufficient evidence to determine whether prophylactic clotting factor concentrates decrease bleeding and bleeding-related complications in patients with hemophilia and existing joint damage; study results are inconsistent.
In patients with hemophilia A without inhibitors, recombinant factor VIII used for acute bleeding episodes stops 95% of bleeds.
BIVV001: A phase 1/2 study of a fusion protein BIVV001 that increases the half-life of Factor VIII safely maintained Factor VIII levels in the normal range for 4 days and at 17% at 7 days.

Efanesoctocog alfa: this is a highly sustained Factor VIII replacement given once weekly. A study gave 74 male children 12 years and older wth severe hemophilia A efanesoctocog alfa once weekly (50 IU/kg) for one year. The median number of annualized bleeding events was 0 and the estimated model-based number was 0.61 (95% CI 0.42-0.90 events); 47 of 74 children had no bleeding episodes and 65 had no spontaneous bleeding episodes. In a phase 3 study in once weekly efanesoctocog alfa was compared with on-demand use; the annualized bleeding rate was lower than with pre-study factor VIII prophylaxis and once weekly was better than on-demand.
Several forms of gene therapy has been successfully used to treat hemophilia A and B.

Valoctocogene roxaparvovec: In a case series of 132 patients, participants received a single infusion of 6×1013 vector genomes of valoctocogene roxaparvovec per kg. The use of Factor VIII decreased by 98.6% and bleeding by 83.8% compared to a pretreatment period. Subsequently, a two year follow-up of this trial found an 85% reduction in the bleeding rate at week 104. Adverse events such as headache, nausea, and elevated hepatic transaminases were common but at 2 years no serious adverse events were reported.

Verbrinacogene setparvovec: this is an adeno-associated virus that increases Factor IX production. Ten patients received a range of doses, and after 27 months all but one had sustained production of Factor IX. All required immunosuppression with glucocorticoids and in some cases tacrolimus as well. One patient with levels 260% of normal had thrombosis of an arteriovenous fistula.

Fidancogene elaparvovec: this is another gene therapy for patients with hemophilia B, found an absolute reduction of 71% in the annual rate of bleeding episodes in a phase 3 trial. Approximately 60% required glucocorticoids for transaminitis or decreased factor IX levels.

Etranacogene dezaparvovec: This is another adeno-associated virus vectored gene therapy for Factor IX (Padua variant). It was given in a dose of 2x 1013/kg to 54 men with hemophilia B currently receiving Factor IX concentrate. The bleeding rate decreased significantly (1.5 vs 4.2/year, p <.001) in a before after analysis.
No clinical trials have evaluated surgery or other procedures in the direct management or supportive care of patients with hemophilia.

When patients are undergoing major surgery they should receive factor concentrate twice daily for 7 to 10 days. Data are insufficient for assessing the most effective and safe hemostatic treatment to prevent bleeding.

Cochrane authors identified two trials supporting use of systemically-administered tranexamic acid and epsilon aminocaproic acid for preventing postoperative bleeding in people with hemophilia undergoing dental extraction.

Thrombotic adverse events after clotting factor concentrate administration are rare. Authors of a systematic review found only 20 thrombotic events reported among 5528 patients with hemophilia A, B or von Willebrand disease; only two were major venous thromboembolic episodes, both in patients with von Willebrand disease on prolonged replacement for surgery. Other types of adverse events following infusion of coagulation factor concentrates are also relatively rare in patients with inherited coagulation disorders; the most common events are allergic.
Fibrin glue and chitosan-based dressings may be useful for local hemostasis in patients with hemophilia undergoing surgical procedures.
Aspirations of hemarthroses are rarely needed since most settle after treatment with concentrate.
Synovectomy may be useful in alleviating symptoms, however because of progressive joint destruction, some patients develop advanced arthropathy requiring joint replacement.

Among patients with hemophilia undergoing knee replacement, 16% developed infection in one study and complications occurred in 31.5% in a meta-analysis of cohort studies. The long-term functional outcomes, however, are generally good. Good long-term outcomes of hip and knee replacement were also seen in another cohort study of 22 patients; hemarthroses were more common in patients with hemophilia than controls (52% vs. 7%, respectively) but infection rates were similar (7% vs. 13%, respectively).
It is not known if patients with hemophilia undergoing knee or hip replacement require thromboembolic prophylaxis as risk of thrombosis is low.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 8 small trials found exercise interventions produced improvement in one or more outcomes including pain, range of motion, strength and walking tolerance. While caution should be used in interpreting findings, hydrotherapy may be more effective than land exercises for pain relief in adults and functional exercises appear more effective than static or short arc exercises for improving muscle strength; data on safety are limited.

Psychological advice may help a patient cope with their disease. Authors of a Cochrane review of 7 trials at high risk of bias (362 participants) found mixed results for psycho-educational interventions and a need for stronger and systematically-reported outcome measures.
In one patient survey of treatment preferences, risk of viral infection was the most important treatment attribute.
Avoid intramuscular injections.
Avoid aspirin and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs.
Intra-articular administration of hyaluronic acid for knee hemophilic arthropathy may improve pain and functional recovery, based on a small case series.

In a study of 10 patients with severe hemophilia B, factor IX gene therapy with a single infusion of self-complementary adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) vector resulted in an increase in circulating factor IX to a level that was near normal over a median period of 3.2 years. In the high-dose group of 6 patients, there was a reduction of more than 90% in both bleeding episodes and the use of prophylactic factor IX concentrate. No late toxic effects from the therapy were observed.
Treatment duration varies depending on site and severity of bleeding.
Bleeds treated very early by the patient at home often only require a single dose of concentrate.
Hospitalize patients with head injury, major trauma, and hemarthroses and muscle hematomas that fail to settle after 24 hours of home treatment.
Also consider hospitalization following surgical or invasive procedures.

Up to 30% of patients with severe hemophilia A develop alloantibodies to factor VIII. In a systematic review, the rates of development of antibodies were 14.3% (10.4%-19.4%) for those on plasma-derived FVIII and 27.4% (23.6%-31.5%) for those on recombinant FVIII; after multivariate analysis, source of concentrate was no longer significant. Other studies have also reported that both plasma-derived products and recombinant products confer a similar risk of inhibitor development.

The development of inhibitory antibodies to factor VIII in people with hemophilia A appears to be a complex process involving some 53 genetic single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Immune system challenges also may contribute to the risk.

The presence of IgG4 antibodies in patients with hemophilia A or B is a strong indicator of the presence an inhibitor to a clotting factor and IgG1 antibodies to factor VIII have been found in the blood of people with hemophilia A before they developed inhibitors.
Patients with inhibitory antibodies should undergo immune tolerance induction (ITI), analogous to allergy desensitization, with regular administration of factor concentrate.
Although there are multiple different regimens, ITI is successful approximately half the time. In one cohort analysis, rituximab increased the likelihood of inhibitor clearance more than ITI.
Regimens for ITI: from 50 IU per day on alternate days to 200 IU per kg per day.
A case series performed in Mexico reported benefit from intra-articular oxytetracycline on joint function and reduced frequency of hemarthroses in children with chronic synovitis.
Patients with mild hemophilia have a normal life expectancy. C

If not infected with HIV, the median life expectancy for patients with hemophilia is 75 years and the risk of death from cardiovascular disease is approximately two thirds that of the general population. C
Untreated severe hemophilia can result in significant disability due to hemophilic arthropathy.
Patients with mild hemophilia have a normal life expectancy.

If not infected with HIV, the median life expectancy for patients with hemophilia is 75 years and the risk of death from cardiovascular disease is approximately two thirds that of the general population.

A 2006 Canadian study found that patients with hemophilia infected with HIV had a life expectancy of 15 years after diagnosis. Patients in this study had been infected between 1982, when HIV became prevalent in the supply of blood products, and 1985, when it was able to be removed. As of 2003, 61% of patients infected with HIV had died, compared with 6.5% of matched patients without HIV.

Patients should be seen every 6 to 12 months at a hemophilia center for an evaluation of bleed frequency and a musculoskeletal assessment. In 2010, there were 32,612 patients being served in US Hemophilia Treatment Centers. Local centers can be found through the National Hemophilia Foundation.

The British Committee for Standards in Haematology recommends that for children on prophylaxis, trough factor levels should be measured at routine clinic visits. In the absence of bleeds, maintenance of trough levels >1 IU/dL is not always necessary.
All patients with hemophilia treated with clotting factors before 1985 should be screened for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV infections.
Patients in their first 50 treatment days with clotting factor should have tests every 3 months to assess for inhibitor antibodies to factor VIII.
Patients with severe hemophilia may have low bone mineral density.
If you are using prophylactic therapy, take your treatment regularly.
Infuse yourself with factor VIII/IX concentrate at the earliest sign of bleeding. The earlier the bleeding is controlled, the less the pain and disability you will have.

If you have mild disease and are not using home treatment, you should go to a facility able to treat you as soon as possible. You should know the location of your nearest treatment center when at home and when you are traveling.

You should avoid sports that may result in head injury, such as boxing. While vigorous activity such as basketball or wrestling confers a transient increased risk of bleeding, the absolute risk appears small. The average boy participating in 3 collision-prone physical activities weekly will only experience 1 additional bleeding episode per year.
Inform all doctors that you have hemophilia. You are likely to be more knowledgeable about hemophilia than most doctors.
Carriers often have factor VIII/IX levels at the lower end of normal.

About 1%-5% of acquired hemophilia A cases affect mothers in the postpartum setting. Authors of a case series of 176 cases found a mean age of 29.9 years; the diagnosis was made at a median of 60 days after delivery (range 0-308 days) and bleeding types were obstetrical (43.4%), cutaneous (41.3%), and muscular (36.7%). FVIII of <1% was found in over 90% and FVIII inhibitor was documented in 75.4% of cases. Six of 24 women who had subsequent pregnancies had evidence of hemophilia A recurrence during that pregnancy.
Hemophilia A carriers with low factor VIII levels usually correct during pregnancy. Hemophilia B carriers with low factor IX levels, however, do not correct during pregnancy.

The following recommendations are based on consensus:
Hemophilia carriers should have their factor VIII/IX levels measured toward the end of pregnancy (eg, 28-32 weeks) so that the management of delivery can be planned. Cell-free DNA testing using maternal plasma can determine fetal gender to identify if a fetus is male and possibly at risk. Chorionic villous sampling between 12 and 16 weeks of pregnancy or amniocentesis between 14 and 20 weeks can confirm a diagnosis through genetic testing. Cell-free fetal DNA analysis in maternal plasma is being validated to allow for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis. Male fetuses should be delivered assuming that they are affected by hemophilia. The mode of delivery should be for obstetric reasons and can be either vaginal or cesarean. Forceps should be avoided in the delivery of at risk male fetuses. A blood sample should be obtained from the umbilical cord from all males born to hemophilia carriers and the sample should be tested for factor VIII/IX. Vitamin K should only be given orally to babies suspected of having hemophilia.
Children younger than 6 months rarely have bleeding problems. Once they become active, bruising and joint bleeds can occur.
Where there is no family history of hemophilia, nonaccidental injury can be considered as a possible diagnosis.
Joint bleeds can be difficult to diagnose in very young children who find it difficult to express themselves.
Bruising is a frequent complaint in young children but is not a common complaint in older individuals.

The use of regular infusions of clotting factor concentrate 2 to 3 times per week prevents bleeds, prevents arthropathy, and leads to improved quality of life in contrast to episodic on-demand therapy which is given only when a bleed develops.
Venous access can be difficult, so a central venous access device should be considered for children using regular home treatment.
